22.8: “‘Who are you, lord?’ I asked. “And the voice replied, ‘I am Jesus the Nazarene, the one you are persecuting.’
22.9: The people with me saw the light but didn’t understand the voice speaking to me.
22.10: “I asked, ‘What should I do, Lord?’ “And the Lord told me, ‘Get up and go into Damascus, and there you will be told everything you are to do.’
22.11: “I was blinded by the intense light and had to be led by the hand to Damascus by my companions.
22.12: A man named Ananias lived there. He was a godly man, deeply devoted to the law, and well regarded by all the Jews of Damascus.
22.13: He came and stood beside me and said, ‘Brother Saul, regain your sight.’ And that very moment I could see him!
22.14: “Then he told me, ‘The God of our ancestors has chosen you to know his will and to see the Righteous One and hear him speak.
22.15: For you are to be his witness, telling everyone what you have seen and heard.
22.16: What are you waiting for? Get up and be baptized. Have your sins washed away by calling on the name of the Lord.’
22.17: “After I returned to Jerusalem, I was praying in the Temple and fell into a trance.
22.18: I saw a vision of Jesus saying to me, ‘Hurry! Leave Jerusalem, for the people here won’t accept your testimony about me.’
22.19: “‘But Lord,’ I argued, ‘they certainly know that in every synagogue I imprisoned and beat those who believed in you.
22.20: And I was in complete agreement when your witness Stephen was killed. I stood by and kept the coats they took off when they stoned him.’
22.21: “But the Lord said to me, ‘Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles!’”
22.22: The crowd listened until Paul said that word. Then they all began to shout, “Away with such a fellow! He isn’t fit to live!”
22.23: They yelled, threw off their coats, and tossed handfuls of dust into the air.
22.24: The commander brought Paul inside and ordered him lashed with whips to make him confess his crime. He wanted to find out why the crowd had become so furious.
22.25: When they tied Paul down to lash him, Paul said to the officer standing there, “Is it legal for you to whip a Roman citizen who hasn’t even been tried?”
22.26: When the officer heard this, he went to the commander and asked, “What are you doing? This man is a Roman citizen!”
22.27: So the commander went over and asked Paul, “Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?” “Yes, I certainly am,” Paul replied.
22.28: “I am, too,” the commander muttered, “and it cost me plenty!” Paul answered, “But I am a citizen by birth!”
22.29: The soldiers who were about to interrogate Paul quickly withdrew when they heard he was a Roman citizen, and the commander was frightened because he had ordered him bound and whipped.
22.30: The next day the commander ordered the leading priests into session with the Jewish high council. He wanted to find out what the trouble was all about, so he released Paul to have him stand before them.

3.1: Peter and John went to the Temple one afternoon to take part in the three o’clock prayer service.
3.2: As they approached the Temple, a man lame from birth was being carried in. Each day he was put beside the Temple gate, the one called the Beautiful Gate, so he could beg from the people going into the Temple.
3.3: When he saw Peter and John about to enter, he asked them for some money.
3.4: Peter and John looked at him intently, and Peter said, “Look at us!”
3.5: The lame man looked at them eagerly, expecting some money.
3.6: But Peter said, “I don’t have any silver or gold for you. But I’ll give you what I have. In the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene, get up and walk!”
3.7: Then Peter took the lame man by the right hand and helped him up. And as he did, the man’s feet and ankles were instantly healed and strengthened.
3.8: He jumped up, stood on his feet, and began to walk! Then, walking, leaping, and praising God, he went into the Temple with them.
3.9: All the people saw him walking and heard him praising God.
3.10: When they realized he was the lame beggar they had seen so often at the Beautiful Gate, they were absolutely astounded!
3.11: They all rushed out in amazement to Solomon’s Colonnade, where the man was holding tightly to Peter and John.
3.12: Peter saw his opportunity and addressed the crowd. “People of Israel,” he said, “what is so surprising about this? And why stare at us as though we had made this man walk by our own power or godliness?
3.13: For it is the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—the God of all our ancestors—who has brought glory to his servant Jesus by doing this. This is the same Jesus whom you handed over and rejected before Pilate, despite Pilate’s decision to release him.
3.14: You rejected this holy, righteous one and instead demanded the release of a murderer.
3.15: You killed the author of life, but God raised him from the dead. And we are witnesses of this fact!
3.16: “Through faith in the name of Jesus, this man was healed—and you know how crippled he was before. Faith in Jesus’ name has healed him before your very eyes.
3.17: “Friends, I realize that what you and your leaders did to Jesus was done in ignorance.
3.18: But God was fulfilling what all the prophets had foretold about the Messiah—that he must suffer these things.
3.19: Now repent of your sins and turn to God, so that your sins may be wiped away.
3.20: Then times of refreshment will come from the presence of the Lord, and he will again send you Jesus, your appointed Messiah.
3.21: For he must remain in heaven until the time for the final restoration of all things, as God promised long ago through his holy prophets.
3.22: Moses said, ‘The Lord your God will raise up for you a Prophet like me from among your own people. Listen carefully to everything he tells you.’
3.23: Then Moses said, ‘Anyone who will not listen to that Prophet will be completely cut off from God’s people.’
3.24: “Starting with Samuel, every prophet spoke about what is happening today.
3.25: You are the children of those prophets, and you are included in the covenant God promised to your ancestors. For God said to Abraham, ‘Through your descendants all the families on earth will be blessed.’
3.26: When God raised up his servant, Jesus, he sent him first to you people of Israel, to bless you by turning each of you back from your sinful ways.”

13.1: Among the prophets and teachers of the church at Antioch of Syria were Barnabas, Simeon (called “the black man”), Lucius (from Cyrene), Manaen (the childhood companion of King Herod Antipas), and Saul.
13.2: One day as these men were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, “Appoint Barnabas and Saul for the special work to which I have called them.”
13.3: So after more fasting and prayer, the men laid their hands on them and sent them on their way.
13.4: So Barnabas and Saul were sent out by the Holy Spirit. They went down to the seaport of Seleucia and then sailed for the island of Cyprus.
13.5: There, in the town of Salamis, they went to the Jewish synagogues and preached the word of God. John Mark went with them as their assistant.
13.6: Afterward they traveled from town to town across the entire island until finally they reached Paphos, where they met a Jewish sorcerer, a false prophet named Bar-Jesus.
13.7: He had attached himself to the governor, Sergius Paulus, who was an intelligent man. The governor invited Barnabas and Saul to visit him, for he wanted to hear the word of God.
13.8: But Elymas, the sorcerer (as his name means in Greek), interfered and urged the governor to pay no attention to what Barnabas and Saul said. He was trying to keep the governor from believing.
13.9: Saul, also known as Paul, was filled with the Holy Spirit, and he looked the sorcerer in the eye.
13.10: Then he said, “You son of the devil, full of every sort of deceit and fraud, and enemy of all that is good! Will you never stop perverting the true ways of the Lord?
13.11: Watch now, for the Lord has laid his hand of punishment upon you, and you will be struck blind. You will not see the sunlight for some time.” Instantly mist and darkness came over the man’s eyes, and he began groping around begging for someone to take his hand and lead him.
13.12: When the governor saw what had happened, he became a believer, for he was astonished at the teaching about the Lord.
13.13: Paul and his companions then left Paphos by ship for Pamphylia, landing at the port town of Perga. There John Mark left them and returned to Jerusalem.
13.14: But Paul and Barnabas traveled inland to Antioch of Pisidia. On the Sabbath they went to the synagogue for the services.
13.15: After the usual readings from the books of Moses and the prophets, those in charge of the service sent them this message: “Brothers, if you have any word of encouragement for the people, come and give it.”
13.16: So Paul stood, lifted his hand to quiet them, and started speaking. “Men of Israel,” he said, “and you God-fearing Gentiles, listen to me.
13.17: “The God of this nation of Israel chose our ancestors and made them multiply and grow strong during their stay in Egypt. Then with a powerful arm he led them out of their slavery.
13.18: He put up with them through forty years of wandering in the wilderness.
13.19: Then he destroyed seven nations in Canaan and gave their land to Israel as an inheritance.
13.20: All this took about 450 years. “After that, God gave them judges to rule until the time of Samuel the prophet.
13.21: Then the people begged for a king, and God gave them Saul son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, who reigned for forty years.
13.22: But God removed Saul and replaced him with David, a man about whom God said, ‘I have found David son of Jesse, a man after my own heart. He will do everything I want him to do.’
13.23: “And it is one of King David’s descendants, Jesus, who is God’s promised Savior of Israel!
13.24: Before he came, John the Baptist preached that all the people of Israel needed to repent of their sins and turn to God and be baptized.
13.25: As John was finishing his ministry he asked, ‘Do you think I am the Messiah? No, I am not! But he is coming soon—and I’m not even worthy to be his slave and untie the sandals on his feet.’
13.26: “Brothers—you sons of Abraham, and also you God-fearing Gentiles—this message of salvation has been sent to us!
13.27: The people in Jerusalem and their leaders did not recognize Jesus as the one the prophets had spoken about. Instead, they condemned him, and in doing this they fulfilled the prophets’ words that are read every Sabbath.
13.28: They found no legal reason to execute him, but they asked Pilate to have him killed anyway.
13.29: “When they had done all that the prophecies said about him, they took him down from the cross and placed him in a tomb.
13.30: But God raised him from the dead!
13.31: And over a period of many days he appeared to those who had gone with him from Galilee to Jerusalem. They are now his witnesses to the people of Israel.
13.32: “And now we are here to bring you this Good News. The promise was made to our ancestors,
13.33: and God has now fulfilled it for us, their descendants, by raising Jesus. This is what the second psalm says about Jesus: ‘You are my Son. Today I have become your Father.’
13.34: For God had promised to raise him from the dead, not leaving him to rot in the grave. He said, ‘I will give you the sacred blessings I promised to David.’
13.35: Another psalm explains it more fully: ‘You will not allow your Holy One to rot in the grave.’
13.36: This is not a reference to David, for after David had done the will of God in his own generation, he died and was buried with his ancestors, and his body decayed.
13.37: No, it was a reference to someone else—someone whom God raised and whose body did not decay.
13.38: “Brothers, listen! We are here to proclaim that through this man Jesus there is forgiveness for your sins.
13.39: Everyone who believes in him is made right in God’s sight—something the law of Moses could never do.
13.40: Be careful! Don’t let the prophets’ words apply to you. For they said,
13.41: ‘Look, you mockers, be amazed and die! For I am doing something in your own day, something you wouldn’t believe even if someone told you about it.’”
13.42: As Paul and Barnabas left the synagogue that day, the people begged them to speak about these things again the next week.
13.43: Many Jews and devout converts to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas, and the two men urged them to continue to rely on the grace of God.
13.44: The following week almost the entire city turned out to hear them preach the word of the Lord.
13.45: But when some of the Jews saw the crowds, they were jealous; so they slandered Paul and argued against whatever he said.
13.46: Then Paul and Barnabas spoke out boldly and declared, “It was necessary that we first preach the word of God to you Jews. But since you have rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, we will offer it to the Gentiles.
13.47: For the Lord gave us this command when he said, ‘I have made you a light to the Gentiles, to bring salvation to the farthest corners of the earth.’”
13.48: When the Gentiles heard this, they were very glad and thanked the Lord for his message; and all who were chosen for eternal life became believers.
13.49: So the Lord’s message spread throughout that region.
13.50: Then the Jews stirred up the influential religious women and the leaders of the city, and they incited a mob against Paul and Barnabas and ran them out of town.
13.51: So they shook the dust from their feet as a sign of rejection and went to the town of Iconium.
13.52: And the believers were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.

25.1: Three days after Festus arrived in Caesarea to take over his new responsibilities, he left for Jerusalem,
25.2: where the leading priests and other Jewish leaders met with him and made their accusations against Paul.
25.3: They asked Festus as a favor to transfer Paul to Jerusalem (planning to ambush and kill him on the way).
25.4: But Festus replied that Paul was at Caesarea and he himself would be returning there soon.
25.5: So he said, “Those of you in authority can return with me. If Paul has done anything wrong, you can make your accusations.”
25.6: About eight or ten days later Festus returned to Caesarea, and on the following day he took his seat in court and ordered that Paul be brought in.
25.7: When Paul arrived, the Jewish leaders from Jerusalem gathered around and made many serious accusations they couldn’t prove.
25.8: Paul denied the charges. “I am not guilty of any crime against the Jewish laws or the Temple or the Roman government,” he said.
25.9: Then Festus, wanting to please the Jews, asked him, “Are you willing to go to Jerusalem and stand trial before me there?”
25.10: But Paul replied, “No! This is the official Roman court, so I ought to be tried right here. You know very well I am not guilty of harming the Jews.
25.11: If I have done something worthy of death, I don’t refuse to die. But if I am innocent, no one has a right to turn me over to these men to kill me. I appeal to Caesar!”
25.12: Festus conferred with his advisers and then replied, “Very well! You have appealed to Caesar, and to Caesar you will go!”
25.13: A few days later King Agrippa arrived with his sister, Bernice, to pay their respects to Festus.
25.14: During their stay of several days, Festus discussed Paul’s case with the king. “There is a prisoner here,” he told him, “whose case was left for me by Felix.
25.15: When I was in Jerusalem, the leading priests and Jewish elders pressed charges against him and asked me to condemn him.
25.16: I pointed out to them that Roman law does not convict people without a trial. They must be given an opportunity to confront their accusers and defend themselves.
25.17: “When his accusers came here for the trial, I didn’t delay. I called the case the very next day and ordered Paul brought in.
25.18: But the accusations made against him weren’t any of the crimes I expected.
25.19: Instead, it was something about their religion and a dead man named Jesus, who Paul insists is alive.
25.20: I was at a loss to know how to investigate these things, so I asked him whether he would be willing to stand trial on these charges in Jerusalem.
25.21: But Paul appealed to have his case decided by the emperor. So I ordered that he be held in custody until I could arrange to send him to Caesar.”
25.22: “I’d like to hear the man myself,” Agrippa said. And Festus replied, “You will—tomorrow!”
25.23: So the next day Agrippa and Bernice arrived at the auditorium with great pomp, accompanied by military officers and prominent men of the city. Festus ordered that Paul be brought in.
25.24: Then Festus said, “King Agrippa and all who are here, this is the man whose death is demanded by all the Jews, both here and in Jerusalem.
25.25: But in my opinion he has done nothing deserving death. However, since he appealed his case to the emperor, I have decided to send him to Rome.
25.26: “But what shall I write the emperor? For there is no clear charge against him. So I have brought him before all of you, and especially you, King Agrippa, so that after we examine him, I might have something to write.
25.27: For it makes no sense to send a prisoner to the emperor without specifying the charges against him!”

24.1: Five days later Ananias, the high priest, arrived with some of the Jewish elders and the lawyer Tertullus, to present their case against Paul to the governor.
24.2: When Paul was called in, Tertullus presented the charges against Paul in the following address to the governor: “You have provided a long period of peace for us Jews and with foresight have enacted reforms for us.
24.3: For all of this, Your Excellency, we are very grateful to you.
24.4: But I don’t want to bore you, so please give me your attention for only a moment.
24.5: We have found this man to be a troublemaker who is constantly stirring up riots among the Jews all over the world. He is a ringleader of the cult known as the Nazarenes.
24.6: Furthermore, he was trying to desecrate the Temple when we arrested him.
24.8: You can find out the truth of our accusations by examining him yourself.”
24.9: Then the other Jews chimed in, declaring that everything Tertullus said was true.
24.10: The governor then motioned for Paul to speak. Paul said, “I know, sir, that you have been a judge of Jewish affairs for many years, so I gladly present my defense before you.
24.11: You can quickly discover that I arrived in Jerusalem no more than twelve days ago to worship at the Temple.
24.12: My accusers never found me arguing with anyone in the Temple, nor stirring up a riot in any synagogue or on the streets of the city.
24.13: These men cannot prove the things they accuse me of doing.
24.14: “But I admit that I follow the Way, which they call a cult. I worship the God of our ancestors, and I firmly believe the Jewish law and everything written in the prophets.
24.15: I have the same hope in God that these men have, that he will raise both the righteous and the unrighteous.
24.16: Because of this, I always try to maintain a clear conscience before God and all people.
24.17: “After several years away, I returned to Jerusalem with money to aid my people and to offer sacrifices to God.
24.18: My accusers saw me in the Temple as I was completing a purification ceremony. There was no crowd around me and no rioting.
24.19: But some Jews from the province of Asia were there—and they ought to be here to bring charges if they have anything against me!
24.20: Ask these men here what crime the Jewish high council found me guilty of,
24.21: except for the one time I shouted out, ‘I am on trial before you today because I believe in the resurrection of the dead!’”
24.22: At that point Felix, who was quite familiar with the Way, adjourned the hearing and said, “Wait until Lysias, the garrison commander, arrives. Then I will decide the case.”
24.23: He ordered an officer to keep Paul in custody but to give him some freedom and allow his friends to visit him and take care of his needs.
24.24: A few days later Felix came back with his wife, Drusilla, who was Jewish. Sending for Paul, they listened as he told them about faith in Christ Jesus.
24.25: As he reasoned with them about righteousness and self-control and the coming day of judgment, Felix became frightened. “Go away for now,” he replied. “When it is more convenient, I’ll call for you again.”
24.26: He also hoped that Paul would bribe him, so he sent for him quite often and talked with him.
24.27: After two years went by in this way, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus. And because Felix wanted to gain favor with the Jewish people, he left Paul in prison.
24.7: Footnote: Some manuscripts add an expanded conclusion to verse 6, all of verse 7, and an additional phrase in verse 8: We would have judged him by our law, 7but Lysias, the commander of the garrison, came and violently took him away from us, 8commanding his accusers to come before you.

12.1: About that time King Herod Agrippa began to persecute some believers in the church.
12.2: He had the apostle James (John’s brother) killed with a sword.
12.3: When Herod saw how much this pleased the Jewish people, he also arrested Peter. (This took place during the Passover celebration.)
12.4: Then he imprisoned him, placing him under the guard of four squads of four soldiers each. Herod intended to bring Peter out for public trial after the Passover.
12.5: But while Peter was in prison, the church prayed very earnestly for him.
12.6: The night before Peter was to be placed on trial, he was asleep, fastened with two chains between two soldiers. Others stood guard at the prison gate.
12.7: Suddenly, there was a bright light in the cell, and an angel of the Lord stood before Peter. The angel struck him on the side to awaken him and said, “Quick! Get up!” And the chains fell off his wrists.
12.8: Then the angel told him, “Get dressed and put on your sandals.” And he did. “Now put on your coat and follow me,” the angel ordered.
12.9: So Peter left the cell, following the angel. But all the time he thought it was a vision. He didn’t realize it was actually happening.
12.10: They passed the first and second guard posts and came to the iron gate leading to the city, and this opened for them all by itself. So they passed through and started walking down the street, and then the angel suddenly left him.
12.11: Peter finally came to his senses. “It’s really true!” he said. “The Lord has sent his angel and saved me from Herod and from what the Jewish leaders had planned to do to me!”
12.12: When he realized this, he went to the home of Mary, the mother of John Mark, where many were gathered for prayer.
12.13: He knocked at the door in the gate, and a servant girl named Rhoda came to open it.
12.14: When she recognized Peter’s voice, she was so overjoyed that, instead of opening the door, she ran back inside and told everyone, “Peter is standing at the door!”
12.15: “You’re out of your mind!” they said. When she insisted, they decided, “It must be his angel.”
12.16: Meanwhile, Peter continued knocking. When they finally opened the door and saw him, they were amazed.
12.17: He motioned for them to quiet down and told them how the Lord had led him out of prison. “Tell James and the other brothers what happened,” he said. And then he went to another place.
12.18: At dawn there was a great commotion among the soldiers about what had happened to Peter.
12.19: Herod Agrippa ordered a thorough search for him. When he couldn’t be found, Herod interrogated the guards and sentenced them to death. Afterward Herod left Judea to stay in Caesarea for a while.
12.20: Now Herod was very angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon. So they sent a delegation to make peace with him because their cities were dependent upon Herod’s country for food. The delegates won the support of Blastus, Herod’s personal assistant,
12.21: and an appointment with Herod was granted. When the day arrived, Herod put on his royal robes, sat on his throne, and made a speech to them.
12.22: The people gave him a great ovation, shouting, “It’s the voice of a god, not of a man!”
12.23: Instantly, an angel of the Lord struck Herod with a sickness, because he accepted the people’s worship instead of giving the glory to God. So he was consumed with worms and died.
12.24: Meanwhile, the word of God continued to spread, and there were many new believers.
12.25: When Barnabas and Saul had finished their mission to Jerusalem, they returned, taking John Mark with them.

2.1: On the day of Pentecost all the believers were meeting together in one place.
2.2: Suddenly, there was a sound from heaven like the roaring of a mighty windstorm, and it filled the house where they were sitting.
2.3: Then, what looked like flames or tongues of fire appeared and settled on each of them.
2.4: And everyone present was filled with the Holy Spirit and began speaking in other languages, as the Holy Spirit gave them this ability.
2.5: At that time there were devout Jews from every nation living in Jerusalem.
2.6: When they heard the loud noise, everyone came running, and they were bewildered to hear their own languages being spoken by the believers.
2.7: They were completely amazed. “How can this be?” they exclaimed. “These people are all from Galilee,
2.8: and yet we hear them speaking in our own native languages!
2.9: Here we are—Parthians, Medes, Elamites, people from Mesopotamia, Judea, Cappadocia, Pontus, the province of Asia,
2.10: Phrygia, Pamphylia, Egypt, and the areas of Libya around Cyrene, visitors from Rome
2.11: (both Jews and converts to Judaism), Cretans, and Arabs. And we all hear these people speaking in our own languages about the wonderful things God has done!”
2.12: They stood there amazed and perplexed. “What can this mean?” they asked each other.
2.13: But others in the crowd ridiculed them, saying, “They’re just drunk, that’s all!”
2.14: Then Peter stepped forward with the eleven other apostles and shouted to the crowd, “Listen carefully, all of you, fellow Jews and residents of Jerusalem! Make no mistake about this.
2.15: These people are not drunk, as some of you are assuming. Nine o’clock in the morning is much too early for that.
2.16: No, what you see was predicted long ago by the prophet Joel:
2.17: ‘In the last days,’ God says, ‘I will pour out my Spirit upon all people. Your sons and daughters will prophesy. Your young men will see visions, and your old men will dream dreams.
2.18: In those days I will pour out my Spirit even on my servants—men and women alike— and they will prophesy.
2.19: And I will cause wonders in the heavens above and signs on the earth below— blood and fire and clouds of smoke.
2.20: The sun will become dark, and the moon will turn blood red before that great and glorious day of the Lord arrives.
2.21: But everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.’
2.22: “People of Israel, listen! God publicly endorsed Jesus the Nazarene by doing powerful miracles, wonders, and signs through him, as you well know.
2.23: But God knew what would happen, and his prearranged plan was carried out when Jesus was betrayed. With the help of lawless Gentiles, you nailed him to a cross and killed him.
2.24: But God released him from the horrors of death and raised him back to life, for death could not keep him in its grip.
2.25: King David said this about him: ‘I see that the Lord is always with me. I will not be shaken, for he is right beside me.
2.26: No wonder my heart is glad, and my tongue shouts his praises! My body rests in hope.
2.27: For you will not leave my soul among the dead or allow your Holy One to rot in the grave.
2.28: You have shown me the way of life, and you will fill me with the joy of your presence.’
2.29: “Dear brothers, think about this! You can be sure that the patriarch David wasn’t referring to himself, for he died and was buried, and his tomb is still here among us.
2.30: But he was a prophet, and he knew God had promised with an oath that one of David’s own descendants would sit on his throne.
2.31: David was looking into the future and speaking of the Messiah’s resurrection. He was saying that God would not leave him among the dead or allow his body to rot in the grave.
2.32: “God raised Jesus from the dead, and we are all witnesses of this.
2.33: Now he is exalted to the place of highest honor in heaven, at God’s right hand. And the Father, as he had promised, gave him the Holy Spirit to pour out upon us, just as you see and hear today.
2.34: For David himself never ascended into heaven, yet he said, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit in the place of honor at my right hand
2.35: until I humble your enemies, making them a footstool under your feet.”’
2.36: “So let everyone in Israel know for certain that God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, to be both Lord and Messiah!”
2.37: Peter’s words pierced their hearts, and they said to him and to the other apostles, “Brothers, what should we do?”
2.38: Peter replied, “Each of you must repent of your sins and turn to God, and be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins. Then you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.
2.39: This promise is to you, to your children, and to those far away—all who have been called by the Lord our God.”
2.40: Then Peter continued preaching for a long time, strongly urging all his listeners, “Save yourselves from this crooked generation!”
2.41: Those who believed what Peter said were baptized and added to the church that day—about 3,000 in all.
2.42: All the believers devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching, and to fellowship, and to sharing in meals (including the Lord’s Supper), and to prayer.
2.43: A deep sense of awe came over them all, and the apostles performed many miraculous signs and wonders.
2.44: And all the believers met together in one place and shared everything they had.
2.45: They sold their property and possessions and shared the money with those in need.
2.46: They worshiped together at the Temple each day, met in homes for the Lord’s Supper, and shared their meals with great joy and generosity—
2.47: all the while praising God and enjoying the goodwill of all the people. And each day the Lord added to their fellowship those who were being saved.

28.1: Once we were safe on shore, we learned that we were on the island of Malta.
28.2: The people of the island were very kind to us. It was cold and rainy, so they built a fire on the shore to welcome us.
28.3: As Paul gathered an armful of sticks and was laying them on the fire, a poisonous snake, driven out by the heat, bit him on the hand.
28.4: The people of the island saw it hanging from his hand and said to each other, “A murderer, no doubt! Though he escaped the sea, justice will not permit him to live.”
28.5: But Paul shook off the snake into the fire and was unharmed.
28.6: The people waited for him to swell up or suddenly drop dead. But when they had waited a long time and saw that he wasn’t harmed, they changed their minds and decided he was a god.
28.7: Near the shore where we landed was an estate belonging to Publius, the chief official of the island. He welcomed us and treated us kindly for three days.
28.8: As it happened, Publius’s father was ill with fever and dysentery. Paul went in and prayed for him, and laying his hands on him, he healed him.
28.9: Then all the other sick people on the island came and were healed.
28.10: As a result we were showered with honors, and when the time came to sail, people supplied us with everything we would need for the trip.
28.11: It was three months after the shipwreck that we set sail on another ship that had wintered at the island—an Alexandrian ship with the twin gods as its figurehead.
28.12: Our first stop was Syracuse, where we stayed three days.
28.13: From there we sailed across to Rhegium. A day later a south wind began blowing, so the following day we sailed up the coast to Puteoli.
28.14: There we found some believers, who invited us to spend a week with them. And so we came to Rome.
28.15: The brothers and sisters in Rome had heard we were coming, and they came to meet us at the Forum on the Appian Way. Others joined us at The Three Taverns. When Paul saw them, he was encouraged and thanked God.
28.16: When we arrived in Rome, Paul was permitted to have his own private lodging, though he was guarded by a soldier.
28.17: Three days after Paul’s arrival, he called together the local Jewish leaders. He said to them, “Brothers, I was arrested in Jerusalem and handed over to the Roman government, even though I had done nothing against our people or the customs of our ancestors.
28.18: The Romans tried me and wanted to release me, because they found no cause for the death sentence.
28.19: But when the Jewish leaders protested the decision, I felt it necessary to appeal to Caesar, even though I had no desire to press charges against my own people.
28.20: I asked you to come here today so we could get acquainted and so I could explain to you that I am bound with this chain because I believe that the hope of Israel—the Messiah—has already come.”
28.21: They replied, “We have had no letters from Judea or reports against you from anyone who has come here.
28.22: But we want to hear what you believe, for the only thing we know about this movement is that it is denounced everywhere.”
28.23: So a time was set, and on that day a large number of people came to Paul’s lodging. He explained and testified about the Kingdom of God and tried to persuade them about Jesus from the Scriptures. Using the law of Moses and the books of the prophets, he spoke to them from morning until evening.
28.24: Some were persuaded by the things he said, but others did not believe.
28.25: And after they had argued back and forth among themselves, they left with this final word from Paul: “The Holy Spirit was right when he said to your ancestors through Isaiah the prophet,
28.26: ‘Go and say to this people: When you hear what I say, you will not understand. When you see what I do, you will not comprehend.
28.27: For the hearts of these people are hardened, and their ears cannot hear, and they have closed their eyes— so their eyes cannot see, and their ears cannot hear, and their hearts cannot understand, and they cannot turn to me and let me heal them.’
28.28: So I want you to know that this salvation from God has also been offered to the Gentiles, and they will accept it.”
28.30: For the next two years, Paul lived in Rome at his own expense. He welcomed all who visited him,
28.31: boldly proclaiming the Kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ. And no one tried to stop him.
28.29: Footnote: Some manuscripts add verse 29, And when he had said these words, the Jews departed, greatly disagreeing with each other.

11.1: Soon the news reached the apostles and other believers in Judea that the Gentiles had received the word of God.
11.2: But when Peter arrived back in Jerusalem, the Jewish believers criticized him.
11.3: “You entered the home of Gentiles and even ate with them!” they said.
11.4: Then Peter told them exactly what had happened.
11.5: “I was in the town of Joppa,” he said, “and while I was praying, I went into a trance and saw a vision. Something like a large sheet was let down by its four corners from the sky. And it came right down to me.
11.6: When I looked inside the sheet, I saw all sorts of tame and wild animals, reptiles, and birds.
11.7: And I heard a voice say, ‘Get up, Peter; kill and eat them.’
11.8: “‘No, Lord,’ I replied. ‘I have never eaten anything that our Jewish laws have declared impure or unclean.’
11.9: “But the voice from heaven spoke again: ‘Do not call something unclean if God has made it clean.’
11.10: This happened three times before the sheet and all it contained was pulled back up to heaven.
11.11: “Just then three men who had been sent from Caesarea arrived at the house where we were staying.
11.12: The Holy Spirit told me to go with them and not to worry that they were Gentiles. These six brothers here accompanied me, and we soon entered the home of the man who had sent for us.
11.13: He told us how an angel had appeared to him in his home and had told him, ‘Send messengers to Joppa, and summon a man named Simon Peter.
11.14: He will tell you how you and everyone in your household can be saved!’
11.15: “As I began to speak,” Peter continued, “the Holy Spirit fell on them, just as he fell on us at the beginning.
11.16: Then I thought of the Lord’s words when he said, ‘John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.’
11.17: And since God gave these Gentiles the same gift he gave us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I to stand in God’s way?”
11.18: When the others heard this, they stopped objecting and began praising God. They said, “We can see that God has also given the Gentiles the privilege of repenting of their sins and receiving eternal life.”
11.19: Meanwhile, the believers who had been scattered during the persecution after Stephen’s death traveled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch of Syria. They preached the word of God, but only to Jews.
11.20: However, some of the believers who went to Antioch from Cyprus and Cyrene began preaching to the Gentiles about the Lord Jesus.
11.21: The power of the Lord was with them, and a large number of these Gentiles believed and turned to the Lord.
11.22: When the church at Jerusalem heard what had happened, they sent Barnabas to Antioch.
11.23: When he arrived and saw this evidence of God’s blessing, he was filled with joy, and he encouraged the believers to stay true to the Lord.
11.24: Barnabas was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and strong in faith. And many people were brought to the Lord.
11.25: Then Barnabas went on to Tarsus to look for Saul.
11.26: When he found him, he brought him back to Antioch. Both of them stayed there with the church for a full year, teaching large crowds of people. (It was at Antioch that the believers were first called Christians.)
11.27: During this time some prophets traveled from Jerusalem to Antioch.
11.28: One of them named Agabus stood up in one of the meetings and predicted by the Spirit that a great famine was coming upon the entire Roman world. (This was fulfilled during the reign of Claudius.)
11.29: So the believers in Antioch decided to send relief to the brothers and sisters in Judea, everyone giving as much as they could.
11.30: This they did, entrusting their gifts to Barnabas and Saul to take to the elders of the church in Jerusalem.

1.1: In my first book I told you, Theophilus, about everything Jesus began to do and teach
1.2: until the day he was taken up to heaven after giving his chosen apostles further instructions through the Holy Spirit.
1.3: During the forty days after he suffered and died, he appeared to the apostles from time to time, and he proved to them in many ways that he was actually alive. And he talked to them about the Kingdom of God.
1.4: Once when he was eating with them, he commanded them, “Do not leave Jerusalem until the Father sends you the gift he promised, as I told you before.
1.5: John baptized with water, but in just a few days you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.”
1.6: So when the apostles were with Jesus, they kept asking him, “Lord, has the time come for you to free Israel and restore our kingdom?”
1.7: He replied, “The Father alone has the authority to set those dates and times, and they are not for you to know.
1.8: But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you. And you will be my witnesses, telling people about me everywhere—in Jerusalem, throughout Judea, in Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.”
1.9: After saying this, he was taken up into a cloud while they were watching, and they could no longer see him.
1.10: As they strained to see him rising into heaven, two white-robed men suddenly stood among them.
1.11: “Men of Galilee,” they said, “why are you standing here staring into heaven? Jesus has been taken from you into heaven, but someday he will return from heaven in the same way you saw him go!”
1.12: Then the apostles returned to Jerusalem from the Mount of Olives, a distance of half a mile.
1.13: When they arrived, they went to the upstairs room of the house where they were staying. Here are the names of those who were present: Peter, John, James, Andrew, Philip, Thomas, Bartholomew, Matthew, James (son of Alphaeus), Simon (the zealot), and Judas (son of James).
1.14: They all met together and were constantly united in prayer, along with Mary the mother of Jesus, several other women, and the brothers of Jesus.
1.15: During this time, when about 120 believers were together in one place, Peter stood up and addressed them.
1.16: “Brothers,” he said, “the Scriptures had to be fulfilled concerning Judas, who guided those who arrested Jesus. This was predicted long ago by the Holy Spirit, speaking through King David.
1.17: Judas was one of us and shared in the ministry with us.”
1.18: (Judas had bought a field with the money he received for his treachery. Falling headfirst there, his body split open, spilling out all his intestines.
1.19: The news of his death spread to all the people of Jerusalem, and they gave the place the Aramaic name Akeldama, which means “Field of Blood.”)
1.20: Peter continued, “This was written in the book of Psalms, where it says, ‘Let his home become desolate, with no one living in it.’ It also says, ‘Let someone else take his position.’
1.21: “So now we must choose a replacement for Judas from among the men who were with us the entire time we were traveling with the Lord Jesus—
1.22: from the time he was baptized by John until the day he was taken from us. Whoever is chosen will join us as a witness of Jesus’ resurrection.”
1.23: So they nominated two men: Joseph called Barsabbas (also known as Justus) and Matthias.
1.24: Then they all prayed, “O Lord, you know every heart. Show us which of these men you have chosen
1.25: as an apostle to replace Judas in this ministry, for he has deserted us and gone where he belongs.”
1.26: Then they cast lots, and Matthias was selected to become an apostle with the other eleven.

27.1: When the time came, we set sail for Italy. Paul and several other prisoners were placed in the custody of a Roman officer named Julius, a captain of the Imperial Regiment.
27.2: Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica, was also with us. We left on a ship whose home port was Adramyttium on the northwest coast of the province of Asia; it was scheduled to make several stops at ports along the coast of the province.
27.3: The next day when we docked at Sidon, Julius was very kind to Paul and let him go ashore to visit with friends so they could provide for his needs.
27.4: Putting out to sea from there, we encountered strong headwinds that made it difficult to keep the ship on course, so we sailed north of Cyprus between the island and the mainland.
27.5: Keeping to the open sea, we passed along the coast of Cilicia and Pamphylia, landing at Myra, in the province of Lycia.
27.6: There the commanding officer found an Egyptian ship from Alexandria that was bound for Italy, and he put us on board.
27.7: We had several days of slow sailing, and after great difficulty we finally neared Cnidus. But the wind was against us, so we sailed across to Crete and along the sheltered coast of the island, past the cape of Salmone.
27.8: We struggled along the coast with great difficulty and finally arrived at Fair Havens, near the town of Lasea.
27.9: We had lost a lot of time. The weather was becoming dangerous for sea travel because it was so late in the fall, and Paul spoke to the ship’s officers about it.
27.10: “Men,” he said, “I believe there is trouble ahead if we go on—shipwreck, loss of cargo, and danger to our lives as well.”
27.11: But the officer in charge of the prisoners listened more to the ship’s captain and the owner than to Paul.
27.12: And since Fair Havens was an exposed harbor—a poor place to spend the winter—most of the crew wanted to go on to Phoenix, farther up the coast of Crete, and spend the winter there. Phoenix was a good harbor with only a southwest and northwest exposure.
27.13: When a light wind began blowing from the south, the sailors thought they could make it. So they pulled up anchor and sailed close to the shore of Crete.
27.14: But the weather changed abruptly, and a wind of typhoon strength (called a “northeaster”) burst across the island and blew us out to sea.
27.15: The sailors couldn’t turn the ship into the wind, so they gave up and let it run before the gale.
27.16: We sailed along the sheltered side of a small island named Cauda, where with great difficulty we hoisted aboard the lifeboat being towed behind us.
27.17: Then the sailors bound ropes around the hull of the ship to strengthen it. They were afraid of being driven across to the sandbars of Syrtis off the African coast, so they lowered the sea anchor to slow the ship and were driven before the wind.
27.18: The next day, as gale-force winds continued to batter the ship, the crew began throwing the cargo overboard.
27.19: The following day they even took some of the ship’s gear and threw it overboard.
27.20: The terrible storm raged for many days, blotting out the sun and the stars, until at last all hope was gone.
27.21: No one had eaten for a long time. Finally, Paul called the crew together and said, “Men, you should have listened to me in the first place and not left Crete. You would have avoided all this damage and loss.
27.22: But take courage! None of you will lose your lives, even though the ship will go down.
27.23: For last night an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I serve stood beside me,
27.24: and he said, ‘Don’t be afraid, Paul, for you will surely stand trial before Caesar! What’s more, God in his goodness has granted safety to everyone sailing with you.’
27.25: So take courage! For I believe God. It will be just as he said.
27.26: But we will be shipwrecked on an island.”
27.27: About midnight on the fourteenth night of the storm, as we were being driven across the Sea of Adria, the sailors sensed land was near.
27.28: They dropped a weighted line and found that the water was 120 feet deep. But a little later they measured again and found it was only 90 feet deep.
27.29: At this rate they were afraid we would soon be driven against the rocks along the shore, so they threw out four anchors from the back of the ship and prayed for daylight.
27.30: Then the sailors tried to abandon the ship; they lowered the lifeboat as though they were going to put out anchors from the front of the ship.
27.31: But Paul said to the commanding officer and the soldiers, “You will all die unless the sailors stay aboard.”
27.32: So the soldiers cut the ropes to the lifeboat and let it drift away.
27.33: Just as day was dawning, Paul urged everyone to eat. “You have been so worried that you haven’t touched food for two weeks,” he said.
27.34: “Please eat something now for your own good. For not a hair of your heads will perish.”
27.35: Then he took some bread, gave thanks to God before them all, and broke off a piece and ate it.
27.36: Then everyone was encouraged and began to eat—
27.37: all 276 of us who were on board.
27.38: After eating, the crew lightened the ship further by throwing the cargo of wheat overboard.
27.39: When morning dawned, they didn’t recognize the coastline, but they saw a bay with a beach and wondered if they could get to shore by running the ship aground.
27.40: So they cut off the anchors and left them in the sea. Then they lowered the rudders, raised the foresail, and headed toward shore.
27.41: But they hit a shoal and ran the ship aground too soon. The bow of the ship stuck fast, while the stern was repeatedly smashed by the force of the waves and began to break apart.
27.42: The soldiers wanted to kill the prisoners to make sure they didn’t swim ashore and escape.
27.43: But the commanding officer wanted to spare Paul, so he didn’t let them carry out their plan. Then he ordered all who could swim to jump overboard first and make for land.
27.44: The others held on to planks or debris from the broken ship. So everyone escaped safely to shore.

26.1: Then Agrippa said to Paul, “You may speak in your defense.” So Paul, gesturing with his hand, started his defense:
26.2: “I am fortunate, King Agrippa, that you are the one hearing my defense today against all these accusations made by the Jewish leaders,
26.3: for I know you are an expert on all Jewish customs and controversies. Now please listen to me patiently!
26.4: “As the Jewish leaders are well aware, I was given a thorough Jewish training from my earliest childhood among my own people and in Jerusalem.
26.5: If they would admit it, they know that I have been a member of the Pharisees, the strictest sect of our religion.
26.6: Now I am on trial because of my hope in the fulfillment of God’s promise made to our ancestors.
26.7: In fact, that is why the twelve tribes of Israel zealously worship God night and day, and they share the same hope I have. Yet, Your Majesty, they accuse me for having this hope!
26.8: Why does it seem incredible to any of you that God can raise the dead?
26.9: “I used to believe that I ought to do everything I could to oppose the very name of Jesus the Nazarene.
26.10: Indeed, I did just that in Jerusalem. Authorized by the leading priests, I caused many believers there to be sent to prison. And I cast my vote against them when they were condemned to death.
26.11: Many times I had them punished in the synagogues to get them to curse Jesus. I was so violently opposed to them that I even chased them down in foreign cities.
26.12: “One day I was on such a mission to Damascus, armed with the authority and commission of the leading priests.
26.13: About noon, Your Majesty, as I was on the road, a light from heaven brighter than the sun shone down on me and my companions.
26.14: We all fell down, and I heard a voice saying to me in Aramaic, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is useless for you to fight against my will.’
26.15: “‘Who are you, lord?’ I asked. “And the Lord replied, ‘I am Jesus, the one you are persecuting.
26.16: Now get to your feet! For I have appeared to you to appoint you as my servant and witness. Tell people that you have seen me, and tell them what I will show you in the future.
26.17: And I will rescue you from both your own people and the Gentiles. Yes, I am sending you to the Gentiles
26.18: to open their eyes, so they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God. Then they will receive forgiveness for their sins and be given a place among God’s people, who are set apart by faith in me.’
26.19: “And so, King Agrippa, I obeyed that vision from heaven.
26.20: I preached first to those in Damascus, then in Jerusalem and throughout all Judea, and also to the Gentiles, that all must repent of their sins and turn to God—and prove they have changed by the good things they do.
26.21: Some Jews arrested me in the Temple for preaching this, and they tried to kill me.
26.22: But God has protected me right up to this present time so I can testify to everyone, from the least to the greatest. I teach nothing except what the prophets and Moses said would happen—
26.23: that the Messiah would suffer and be the first to rise from the dead, and in this way announce God’s light to Jews and Gentiles alike.”
26.24: Suddenly, Festus shouted, “Paul, you are insane. Too much study has made you crazy!”
26.25: But Paul replied, “I am not insane, Most Excellent Festus. What I am saying is the sober truth.
26.26: And King Agrippa knows about these things. I speak boldly, for I am sure these events are all familiar to him, for they were not done in a corner!
26.27: King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know you do—”
26.28: Agrippa interrupted him. “Do you think you can persuade me to become a Christian so quickly?”
26.29: Paul replied, “Whether quickly or not, I pray to God that both you and everyone here in this audience might become the same as I am, except for these chains.”
26.30: Then the king, the governor, Bernice, and all the others stood and left.
26.31: As they went out, they talked it over and agreed, “This man hasn’t done anything to deserve death or imprisonment.”
26.32: And Agrippa said to Festus, “He could have been set free if he hadn’t appealed to Caesar.”

10.1: In Caesarea there lived a Roman army officer named Cornelius, who was a captain of the Italian Regiment.
10.2: He was a devout, God-fearing man, as was everyone in his household. He gave generously to the poor and prayed regularly to God.
10.3: One afternoon about three o’clock, he had a vision in which he saw an angel of God coming toward him. “Cornelius!” the angel said.
10.4: Cornelius stared at him in terror. “What is it, sir?” he asked the angel. And the angel replied, “Your prayers and gifts to the poor have been received by God as an offering!
10.5: Now send some men to Joppa, and summon a man named Simon Peter.
10.6: He is staying with Simon, a tanner who lives near the seashore.”
10.7: As soon as the angel was gone, Cornelius called two of his household servants and a devout soldier, one of his personal attendants.
10.8: He told them what had happened and sent them off to Joppa.
10.9: The next day as Cornelius’s messengers were nearing the town, Peter went up on the flat roof to pray. It was about noon,
10.10: and he was hungry. But while a meal was being prepared, he fell into a trance.
10.11: He saw the sky open, and something like a large sheet was let down by its four corners.
10.12: In the sheet were all sorts of animals, reptiles, and birds.
10.13: Then a voice said to him, “Get up, Peter; kill and eat them.”
10.14: “No, Lord,” Peter declared. “I have never eaten anything that our Jewish laws have declared impure and unclean.”
10.15: But the voice spoke again: “Do not call something unclean if God has made it clean.”
10.16: The same vision was repeated three times. Then the sheet was suddenly pulled up to heaven.
10.17: Peter was very perplexed. What could the vision mean? Just then the men sent by Cornelius found Simon’s house. Standing outside the gate,
10.18: they asked if a man named Simon Peter was staying there.
10.19: Meanwhile, as Peter was puzzling over the vision, the Holy Spirit said to him, “Three men have come looking for you.
10.20: Get up, go downstairs, and go with them without hesitation. Don’t worry, for I have sent them.”
10.21: So Peter went down and said, “I’m the man you are looking for. Why have you come?”
10.22: They said, “We were sent by Cornelius, a Roman officer. He is a devout and God-fearing man, well respected by all the Jews. A holy angel instructed him to summon you to his house so that he can hear your message.”
10.23: So Peter invited the men to stay for the night. The next day he went with them, accompanied by some of the brothers from Joppa.
10.24: They arrived in Caesarea the following day. Cornelius was waiting for them and had called together his relatives and close friends.
10.25: As Peter entered his home, Cornelius fell at his feet and worshiped him.
10.26: But Peter pulled him up and said, “Stand up! I’m a human being just like you!”
10.27: So they talked together and went inside, where many others were assembled.
10.28: Peter told them, “You know it is against our laws for a Jewish man to enter a Gentile home like this or to associate with you. But God has shown me that I should no longer think of anyone as impure or unclean.
10.29: So I came without objection as soon as I was sent for. Now tell me why you sent for me.”
10.30: Cornelius replied, “Four days ago I was praying in my house about this same time, three o’clock in the afternoon. Suddenly, a man in dazzling clothes was standing in front of me.
10.31: He told me, ‘Cornelius, your prayer has been heard, and your gifts to the poor have been noticed by God!
10.32: Now send messengers to Joppa, and summon a man named Simon Peter. He is staying in the home of Simon, a tanner who lives near the seashore.’
10.33: So I sent for you at once, and it was good of you to come. Now we are all here, waiting before God to hear the message the Lord has given you.”
10.34: Then Peter replied, “I see very clearly that God shows no favoritism.
10.35: In every nation he accepts those who fear him and do what is right.
10.36: This is the message of Good News for the people of Israel—that there is peace with God through Jesus Christ, who is Lord of all.
10.37: You know what happened throughout Judea, beginning in Galilee, after John began preaching his message of baptism.
10.38: And you know that God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power. Then Jesus went around doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him.
10.39: “And we apostles are witnesses of all he did throughout Judea and in Jerusalem. They put him to death by hanging him on a cross,
10.40: but God raised him to life on the third day. Then God allowed him to appear,
10.41: not to the general public, but to us whom God had chosen in advance to be his witnesses. We were those who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead.
10.42: And he ordered us to preach everywhere and to testify that Jesus is the one appointed by God to be the judge of all—the living and the dead.
10.43: He is the one all the prophets testified about, saying that everyone who believes in him will have their sins forgiven through his name.”
10.44: Even as Peter was saying these things, the Holy Spirit fell upon all who were listening to the message.
10.45: The Jewish believers who came with Peter were amazed that the gift of the Holy Spirit had been poured out on the Gentiles, too.
10.46: For they heard them speaking in other tongues and praising God. Then Peter asked,
10.47: “Can anyone object to their being baptized, now that they have received the Holy Spirit just as we did?”
10.48: So he gave orders for them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Afterward Cornelius asked him to stay with them for several days.

21.1: After saying farewell to the Ephesian elders, we sailed straight to the island of Cos. The next day we reached Rhodes and then went to Patara.
21.2: There we boarded a ship sailing for Phoenicia.
21.3: We sighted the island of Cyprus, passed it on our left, and landed at the harbor of Tyre, in Syria, where the ship was to unload its cargo.
21.4: We went ashore, found the local believers, and stayed with them a week. These believers prophesied through the Holy Spirit that Paul should not go on to Jerusalem.
21.5: When we returned to the ship at the end of the week, the entire congregation, including women and children, left the city and came down to the shore with us. There we knelt, prayed,
21.6: and said our farewells. Then we went aboard, and they returned home.
21.7: The next stop after leaving Tyre was Ptolemais, where we greeted the brothers and sisters and stayed for one day.
21.8: The next day we went on to Caesarea and stayed at the home of Philip the Evangelist, one of the seven men who had been chosen to distribute food.
21.9: He had four unmarried daughters who had the gift of prophecy.
21.10: Several days later a man named Agabus, who also had the gift of prophecy, arrived from Judea.
21.11: He came over, took Paul’s belt, and bound his own feet and hands with it. Then he said, “The Holy Spirit declares, ‘So shall the owner of this belt be bound by the Jewish leaders in Jerusalem and turned over to the Gentiles.’”
21.12: When we heard this, we and the local believers all begged Paul not to go on to Jerusalem.
21.13: But he said, “Why all this weeping? You are breaking my heart! I am ready not only to be jailed at Jerusalem but even to die for the sake of the Lord Jesus.”
21.14: When it was clear that we couldn’t persuade him, we gave up and said, “The Lord’s will be done.”
21.15: After this we packed our things and left for Jerusalem.
21.16: Some believers from Caesarea accompanied us, and they took us to the home of Mnason, a man originally from Cyprus and one of the early believers.
21.17: When we arrived, the brothers and sisters in Jerusalem welcomed us warmly.
21.18: The next day Paul went with us to meet with James, and all the elders of the Jerusalem church were present.
21.19: After greeting them, Paul gave a detailed account of the things God had accomplished among the Gentiles through his ministry.
21.20: After hearing this, they praised God. And then they said, “You know, dear brother, how many thousands of Jews have also believed, and they all follow the law of Moses very seriously.
21.21: But the Jewish believers here in Jerusalem have been told that you are teaching all the Jews who live among the Gentiles to turn their backs on the laws of Moses. They’ve heard that you teach them not to circumcise their children or follow other Jewish customs.
21.22: What should we do? They will certainly hear that you have come.
21.23: “Here’s what we want you to do. We have four men here who have completed their vow.
21.24: Go with them to the Temple and join them in the purification ceremony, paying for them to have their heads ritually shaved. Then everyone will know that the rumors are all false and that you yourself observe the Jewish laws.
21.25: “As for the Gentile believers, they should do what we already told them in a letter: They should abstain from eating food offered to idols, from consuming blood or the meat of strangled animals, and from sexual immorality.”
21.26: So Paul went to the Temple the next day with the other men. They had already started the purification ritual, so he publicly announced the date when their vows would end and sacrifices would be offered for each of them.
21.27: The seven days were almost ended when some Jews from the province of Asia saw Paul in the Temple and roused a mob against him. They grabbed him,
21.28: yelling, “Men of Israel, help us! This is the man who preaches against our people everywhere and tells everybody to disobey the Jewish laws. He speaks against the Temple—and even defiles this holy place by bringing in Gentiles.”
21.29: (For earlier that day they had seen him in the city with Trophimus, a Gentile from Ephesus, and they assumed Paul had taken him into the Temple.)
21.30: The whole city was rocked by these accusations, and a great riot followed. Paul was grabbed and dragged out of the Temple, and immediately the gates were closed behind him.
21.31: As they were trying to kill him, word reached the commander of the Roman regiment that all Jerusalem was in an uproar.
21.32: He immediately called out his soldiers and officers and ran down among the crowd. When the mob saw the commander and the troops coming, they stopped beating Paul.
21.33: Then the commander arrested him and ordered him bound with two chains. He asked the crowd who he was and what he had done.
21.34: Some shouted one thing and some another. Since he couldn’t find out the truth in all the uproar and confusion, he ordered that Paul be taken to the fortress.
21.35: As Paul reached the stairs, the mob grew so violent the soldiers had to lift him to their shoulders to protect him.
21.36: And the crowd followed behind, shouting, “Kill him, kill him!”
21.37: As Paul was about to be taken inside, he said to the commander, “May I have a word with you?” “Do you know Greek?” the commander asked, surprised.
21.38: “Aren’t you the Egyptian who led a rebellion some time ago and took 4,000 members of the Assassins out into the desert?”
21.39: “No,” Paul replied, “I am a Jew and a citizen of Tarsus in Cilicia, which is an important city. Please, let me talk to these people.”
21.40: The commander agreed, so Paul stood on the stairs and motioned to the people to be quiet. Soon a deep silence enveloped the crowd, and he addressed them in their own language, Aramaic.

17.1: Paul and Silas then traveled through the towns of Amphipolis and Apollonia and came to Thessalonica, where there was a Jewish synagogue.
17.2: As was Paul’s custom, he went to the synagogue service, and for three Sabbaths in a row he used the Scriptures to reason with the people.
17.3: He explained the prophecies and proved that the Messiah must suffer and rise from the dead. He said, “This Jesus I’m telling you about is the Messiah.”
17.4: Some of the Jews who listened were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas, along with many God-fearing Greek men and quite a few prominent women.
17.5: But some of the Jews were jealous, so they gathered some troublemakers from the marketplace to form a mob and start a riot. They attacked the home of Jason, searching for Paul and Silas so they could drag them out to the crowd.
17.6: Not finding them there, they dragged out Jason and some of the other believers instead and took them before the city council. “Paul and Silas have caused trouble all over the world,” they shouted, “and now they are here disturbing our city, too.
17.7: And Jason has welcomed them into his home. They are all guilty of treason against Caesar, for they profess allegiance to another king, named Jesus.”
17.8: The people of the city, as well as the city council, were thrown into turmoil by these reports.
17.9: So the officials forced Jason and the other believers to post bond, and then they released them.
17.10: That very night the believers sent Paul and Silas to Berea. When they arrived there, they went to the Jewish synagogue.
17.11: And the people of Berea were more open-minded than those in Thessalonica, and they listened eagerly to Paul’s message. They searched the Scriptures day after day to see if Paul and Silas were teaching the truth.
17.12: As a result, many Jews believed, as did many of the prominent Greek women and men.
17.13: But when some Jews in Thessalonica learned that Paul was preaching the word of God in Berea, they went there and stirred up trouble.
17.14: The believers acted at once, sending Paul on to the coast, while Silas and Timothy remained behind.
17.15: Those escorting Paul went with him all the way to Athens; then they returned to Berea with instructions for Silas and Timothy to hurry and join him.
17.16: While Paul was waiting for them in Athens, he was deeply troubled by all the idols he saw everywhere in the city.
17.17: He went to the synagogue to reason with the Jews and the God-fearing Gentiles, and he spoke daily in the public square to all who happened to be there.
17.18: He also had a debate with some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers. When he told them about Jesus and his resurrection, they said, “What’s this babbler trying to say with these strange ideas he’s picked up?” Others said, “He seems to be preaching about some foreign gods.”
17.19: Then they took him to the high council of the city. “Come and tell us about this new teaching,” they said.
17.20: “You are saying some rather strange things, and we want to know what it’s all about.”
17.21: (It should be explained that all the Athenians as well as the foreigners in Athens seemed to spend all their time discussing the latest ideas.)
17.22: So Paul, standing before the council, addressed them as follows: “Men of Athens, I notice that you are very religious in every way,
17.23: for as I was walking along I saw your many shrines. And one of your altars had this inscription on it: ‘To an Unknown God.’ This God, whom you worship without knowing, is the one I’m telling you about.
17.24: “He is the God who made the world and everything in it. Since he is Lord of heaven and earth, he doesn’t live in man-made temples,
17.25: and human hands can’t serve his needs—for he has no needs. He himself gives life and breath to everything, and he satisfies every need.
17.26: From one man he created all the nations throughout the whole earth. He decided beforehand when they should rise and fall, and he determined their boundaries.
17.27: “His purpose was for the nations to seek after God and perhaps feel their way toward him and find him—though he is not far from any one of us.
17.28: For in him we live and move and exist. As some of your own poets have said, ‘We are his offspring.’
17.29: And since this is true, we shouldn’t think of God as an idol designed by craftsmen from gold or silver or stone.
17.30: “God overlooked people’s ignorance about these things in earlier times, but now he commands everyone everywhere to repent of their sins and turn to him.
17.31: For he has set a day for judging the world with justice by the man he has appointed, and he proved to everyone who this is by raising him from the dead.”
17.32: When they heard Paul speak about the resurrection of the dead, some laughed in contempt, but others said, “We want to hear more about this later.”
17.33: That ended Paul’s discussion with them,
17.34: but some joined him and became believers. Among them were Dionysius, a member of the council, a woman named Damaris, and others with them.

7.1: Then the high priest asked Stephen, “Are these accusations true?”
7.2: This was Stephen’s reply: “Brothers and fathers, listen to me. Our glorious God appeared to our ancestor Abraham in Mesopotamia before he settled in Haran.
7.3: God told him, ‘Leave your native land and your relatives, and come into the land that I will show you.’
7.4: So Abraham left the land of the Chaldeans and lived in Haran until his father died. Then God brought him here to the land where you now live.
7.5: “But God gave him no inheritance here, not even one square foot of land. God did promise, however, that eventually the whole land would belong to Abraham and his descendants—even though he had no children yet.
7.6: God also told him that his descendants would live in a foreign land, where they would be oppressed as slaves for 400 years.
7.7: ‘But I will punish the nation that enslaves them,’ God said, ‘and in the end they will come out and worship me here in this place.’
7.8: “God also gave Abraham the covenant of circumcision at that time. So when Abraham became the father of Isaac, he circumcised him on the eighth day. And the practice was continued when Isaac became the father of Jacob, and when Jacob became the father of the twelve patriarchs of the Israelite nation.
7.9: “These patriarchs were jealous of their brother Joseph, and they sold him to be a slave in Egypt. But God was with him
7.10: and rescued him from all his troubles. And God gave him favor before Pharaoh, king of Egypt. God also gave Joseph unusual wisdom, so that Pharaoh appointed him governor over all of Egypt and put him in charge of the palace.
7.11: “But a famine came upon Egypt and Canaan. There was great misery, and our ancestors ran out of food.
7.12: Jacob heard that there was still grain in Egypt, so he sent his sons—our ancestors—to buy some.
7.13: The second time they went, Joseph revealed his identity to his brothers, and they were introduced to Pharaoh.
7.14: Then Joseph sent for his father, Jacob, and all his relatives to come to Egypt, seventy-five persons in all.
7.15: So Jacob went to Egypt. He died there, as did our ancestors.
7.16: Their bodies were taken to Shechem and buried in the tomb Abraham had bought for a certain price from Hamor’s sons in Shechem.
7.17: “As the time drew near when God would fulfill his promise to Abraham, the number of our people in Egypt greatly increased.
7.18: But then a new king came to the throne of Egypt who knew nothing about Joseph.
7.19: This king exploited our people and oppressed them, forcing parents to abandon their newborn babies so they would die.
7.20: “At that time Moses was born—a beautiful child in God’s eyes. His parents cared for him at home for three months.
7.21: When they had to abandon him, Pharaoh’s daughter adopted him and raised him as her own son.
7.22: Moses was taught all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and he was powerful in both speech and action.
7.23: “One day when Moses was forty years old, he decided to visit his relatives, the people of Israel.
7.24: He saw an Egyptian mistreating an Israelite. So Moses came to the man’s defense and avenged him, killing the Egyptian.
7.25: Moses assumed his fellow Israelites would realize that God had sent him to rescue them, but they didn’t.
7.26: “The next day he visited them again and saw two men of Israel fighting. He tried to be a peacemaker. ‘Men,’ he said, ‘you are brothers. Why are you fighting each other?’
7.27: “But the man in the wrong pushed Moses aside. ‘Who made you a ruler and judge over us?’ he asked.
7.28: ‘Are you going to kill me as you killed that Egyptian yesterday?’
7.29: When Moses heard that, he fled the country and lived as a foreigner in the land of Midian. There his two sons were born.
7.30: “Forty years later, in the desert near Mount Sinai, an angel appeared to Moses in the flame of a burning bush.
7.31: When Moses saw it, he was amazed at the sight. As he went to take a closer look, the voice of the Lord called out to him,
7.32: ‘I am the God of your ancestors—the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.’ Moses shook with terror and did not dare to look.
7.33: “Then the Lord said to him, ‘Take off your sandals, for you are standing on holy ground.
7.34: I have certainly seen the oppression of my people in Egypt. I have heard their groans and have come down to rescue them. Now go, for I am sending you back to Egypt.’
7.35: “So God sent back the same man his people had previously rejected when they demanded, ‘Who made you a ruler and judge over us?’ Through the angel who appeared to him in the burning bush, God sent Moses to be their ruler and savior.
7.36: And by means of many wonders and miraculous signs, he led them out of Egypt, through the Red Sea, and through the wilderness for forty years.
7.37: “Moses himself told the people of Israel, ‘God will raise up for you a Prophet like me from among your own people.’
7.38: Moses was with our ancestors, the assembly of God’s people in the wilderness, when the angel spoke to him at Mount Sinai. And there Moses received life-giving words to pass on to us.
7.39: “But our ancestors refused to listen to Moses. They rejected him and wanted to return to Egypt.
7.40: They told Aaron, ‘Make us some gods who can lead us, for we don’t know what has become of this Moses, who brought us out of Egypt.’
7.41: So they made an idol shaped like a calf, and they sacrificed to it and celebrated over this thing they had made.
7.42: Then God turned away from them and abandoned them to serve the stars of heaven as their gods! In the book of the prophets it is written, ‘Was it to me you were bringing sacrifices and offerings during those forty years in the wilderness, Israel?
7.43: No, you carried your pagan gods— the shrine of Molech, the star of your god Rephan, and the images you made to worship them. So I will send you into exile as far away as Babylon.’
7.44: “Our ancestors carried the Tabernacle with them through the wilderness. It was constructed according to the plan God had shown to Moses.
7.45: Years later, when Joshua led our ancestors in battle against the nations that God drove out of this land, the Tabernacle was taken with them into their new territory. And it stayed there until the time of King David.
7.46: “David found favor with God and asked for the privilege of building a permanent Temple for the God of Jacob.
7.47: But it was Solomon who actually built it.
7.48: However, the Most High doesn’t live in temples made by human hands. As the prophet says,
7.49: ‘Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool. Could you build me a temple as good as that?’ asks the Lord. ‘Could you build me such a resting place?
7.50: Didn’t my hands make both heaven and earth?’
7.51: “You stubborn people! You are heathen at heart and deaf to the truth. Must you forever resist the Holy Spirit? That’s what your ancestors did, and so do you!
7.52: Name one prophet your ancestors didn’t persecute! They even killed the ones who predicted the coming of the Righteous One—the Messiah whom you betrayed and murdered.
7.53: You deliberately disobeyed God’s law, even though you received it from the hands of angels.”
7.54: The Jewish leaders were infuriated by Stephen’s accusation, and they shook their fists at him in rage.
7.55: But Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, gazed steadily into heaven and saw the glory of God, and he saw Jesus standing in the place of honor at God’s right hand.
7.56: And he told them, “Look, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing in the place of honor at God’s right hand!”
7.57: Then they put their hands over their ears and began shouting. They rushed at him
7.58: and dragged him out of the city and began to stone him. His accusers took off their coats and laid them at the feet of a young man named Saul.
7.59: As they stoned him, Stephen prayed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.”
7.60: He fell to his knees, shouting, “Lord, don’t charge them with this sin!” And with that, he died.

6.1: But as the believers rapidly multiplied, there were rumblings of discontent. The Greek-speaking believers complained about the Hebrew-speaking believers, saying that their widows were being discriminated against in the daily distribution of food.
6.2: So the Twelve called a meeting of all the believers. They said, “We apostles should spend our time teaching the word of God, not running a food program.
6.3: And so, brothers, select seven men who are well respected and are full of the Spirit and wisdom. We will give them this responsibility.
6.4: Then we apostles can spend our time in prayer and teaching the word.”
6.5: Everyone liked this idea, and they chose the following: Stephen (a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit), Philip, Procorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolas of Antioch (an earlier convert to the Jewish faith).
6.6: These seven were presented to the apostles, who prayed for them as they laid their hands on them.
6.7: So God’s message continued to spread. The number of believers greatly increased in Jerusalem, and many of the Jewish priests were converted, too.
6.8: Stephen, a man full of God’s grace and power, performed amazing miracles and signs among the people.
6.9: But one day some men from the Synagogue of Freed Slaves, as it was called, started to debate with him. They were Jews from Cyrene, Alexandria, Cilicia, and the province of Asia.
6.10: None of them could stand against the wisdom and the Spirit with which Stephen spoke.
6.11: So they persuaded some men to lie about Stephen, saying, “We heard him blaspheme Moses, and even God.”
6.12: This roused the people, the elders, and the teachers of religious law. So they arrested Stephen and brought him before the high council.
6.13: The lying witnesses said, “This man is always speaking against the holy Temple and against the law of Moses.
6.14: We have heard him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy the Temple and change the customs Moses handed down to us.”
6.15: At this point everyone in the high council stared at Stephen, because his face became as bright as an angel’s.

16.1: Paul went first to Derbe and then to Lystra, where there was a young disciple named Timothy. His mother was a Jewish believer, but his father was a Greek.
16.2: Timothy was well thought of by the believers in Lystra and Iconium,
16.3: so Paul wanted him to join them on their journey. In deference to the Jews of the area, he arranged for Timothy to be circumcised before they left, for everyone knew that his father was a Greek.
16.4: Then they went from town to town, instructing the believers to follow the decisions made by the apostles and elders in Jerusalem.
16.5: So the churches were strengthened in their faith and grew larger every day.
